text: Circus Circus Las Vegas is a hotel and casino located on the northern Las Vegas Strip in Winchester, Nevada, and is owned and operated by Phil Ruffin. The resort includes the largest permanent circus in the world, featuring circus and trapeze acts and carnival games at its Carnival Midway, as well as the Adventuredome, an indoor amusement park. Originally owned by Jay Sarno and Stanley Mallin, Circus Circus opened without a hotel on October 18, 1968, with a casino on the first floor and carnival games on the second floor, making it one of the first family-oriented casinos in Las Vegas. The opening was delayed from August 1, 1968, to October 1, 1968, after the Nevada Gaming Commission initially denied approval due to insufficient funds, though a $1.1 million loan from relatives of Kirk Kerkorian secured preliminary approval. The casino, designed by Rissman and Rissman Associates with R. C. Johnson and Associates as general contractor, featured a steel and concrete tent-shaped roof reaching 90 feet, painted white and hot pink, and included costumed dealers, cocktail waitresses, small pink elephants, trained monkeys, and an elephant named Tanya that pulled slot machine handles and tossed dice. It also had a Diet Buster all-you-can-eat dessert experience and a short-lived publicity stunt involving baby elephants on an overhead tram. The casino attracted 26,000 people within its first eight hours and had 1,000 employees, with Sarno as president and 25% owner and Jud McIntosh with 22%. The property faced financial struggles in its early years due to its lack of a hotel and a $1 admission fee, which was later dropped. The Nevada Gaming Commission required the debt to be paid off before issuing a permanent license, and after a temporary license extension, a permanent one was granted in May 1969. In 1971, the Teamsters' Union pension fund provided a loan to add a hotel, and a 15-story tower with 409 rooms opened in July 1972. Sarno and Mallin were investigated for tax code violations and alleged organized crime connections, including a gift shop concession granted to Anthony Spilotro (Tony Stuart) under the Chicago Outfit. In 1974, Bill Bennett and William Pennington were approved to lease operations from Sarno and Mallin, who remained landlords; they transformed the property into a profitable venture focused on slot machines and middle-class families, despite skepticism about its theme. They added an RV park in 1979 and motel structures in 1980, increasing the total room count to 1,610. In 1983, Bennett and Pennington purchased the property and added a 29-story tower in 1986. The Adventuredome opened in 1993, and a 35-story tower was completed in 1996. The casino has 123,928 sq ft (11,513.3 m²) of space and 3,767 hotel rooms. The resort also includes the small Slots-A-Fun Casino, opened by Sarno in 1971. Circus Circus Enterprises was renamed Mandalay Resort Group in 1999, and MGM Mirage (later MGM Resorts International) acquired it in 2005. MGM planned to build a multibillion-dollar resort on land north of Circus Circus, where El Rancho Vegas once stood, but canceled the project due to the Great Recession. The El Rancho land was later used for MGM's Festival Grounds, which opened in 2015. Out of 10 Strip resorts, Circus Circus was MGM's most popular property among Hispanic tourists and remained popular among families, though it required renovations. It was the oldest Las Vegas property owned by MGM Resorts. In 2019, MGM sold Circus Circus to Phil Ruffin for $825 million, including Festival Grounds, and Ruffin continued to operate it as a budget property, launching a $30 million renovation project extending into 2023. Early plans by Ruffin included a 2,000-seat theater and converting the RV park into a swimming pool complex with a wave machine, sand beaches, and a lazy river, but these features have not been built as of 2026. In January 2025, Ruffin stated he planned to sell Circus Circus to acquire another property, with the combined property of Circus Circus and Festival Grounds totaling 102 acres and potentially selling for up to $5 billion. The front of the casino originally had a 306-foot-long fountain area with water shoots up to four stories and colored lighting, as well as statues and a carousel, which were later removed. The carousel was removed in 1976 to make room for a 123-foot neon roadside sign depicting a clown named Lucky, created by YESCO and one of Las Vegas' most-photographed signs. A sportsbook opened in September 1976 but closed seven months later. In 1977, plans for a parking garage were made, completed in 1978, and Circusland RV Park was added in 1979. Circus Circus Manor, opened in 1980, consists of five three-story motel buildings with 810 rooms. A monorail, the Circus Sky Shuttle, opened in 1981, connecting the main resort to the Manor rooms and was the first automated transit system in the Las Vegas Valley. A $7 million renovation and expansion project began in 1982, adding casino space and a video game arcade, and a valet parking lot replaced the fountains. Additional casino space and a second parking garage were added in 1985, and construction began on the 29-story Circus Skyrise tower. In 1974, the Guinness Book of World Records named Circus Circus the world's largest permanent circus, a distinction it continues to hold. Pink coloring is used throughout the resort. Jo Harris, who previously designed Caesars Palace, was the original interior designer and designed the 1970s two-story Royal Suite with a balcony and the Chapel of the Fountain, which opened in 1975. The two original 15-story towers are connected and known as the Casino Tower. The Hippodrome showroom hosted shows such as Nudes in the Night and Tom Jones, which starred Babette Bardot, and other topless shows like Naked But Nice and Hot Pants Sexplosion, before being walled off and remaining vacant since 2024.

The 1,000-space parking garage was completed in 1978, with the Circusland RV Park added the following year. Circus Circus Manor, which opened in 1980, consists of five three-story motel buildings with a total of 810 rooms, bringing the resort's overall hotel room count to 1,610. A monorail, the Circus Sky Shuttle, was introduced in 1981 and was the first automated transit system in the Las Vegas Valley; its track, located 18 feet above street level, connected the main resort to the Circus Circus Manor rooms. A $7 million renovation and expansion project began in 1982, adding casino space and a video game arcade, and a valet parking lot was installed in front of the resort, replacing the fountains. In 1985, additional casino space and a second parking garage were added, and construction started on the 29-story Circus Skyrise tower, which would add 1,188 rooms for a total of 2,793, along with more casino space and a sportsbook and a third parking garage. The general contractor was Marnell Corrao Associates, with Veldon Simpson as the architect; groundbreaking occurred on January 31, 1985, and the tower was topped off on September 25, 1985, opening the following year on land previously occupied by the Savoy Motel. A $100 million renovation began in 1996, including the December opening of the $60 million, 35-story West Tower, which added about 1,000 rooms for a total of approximately 3,700. The older rooms were refurbished, and a retail area with 14 shops opened in January 1997. Monorail operations ended around 2000 due to high maintenance costs, though the track remains intact. Most of Montyne's statues were disposed of in 2006 under MGM's ownership, as they were in a state of deterioration. In 2012, Circus Circus introduced an exhibit dedicated to animator Chuck Jones. The midway includes a video game arcade and carnival-type games, features clown shows and trapeze acts several times a day, and clowns roam the resort to amuse visitors; for decades, it included a carousel that operated as a bar. Hotel rooms were renovated in 2014, and the RV park was briefly closed and renovated, with part of it converted into space for MGM's Festival Grounds, leaving 170 spaces; the RV park covers 10 acres and is the only one on the Las Vegas Strip. In 2017, Circus Circus added the Splash Zone water park for hotel guests after several years of planning. By 2022, the pool area had been enlarged as part of Ruffin's $30 million renovation, which included a $10 million update of the elevators and a new paint job emphasizing the circus theme, as well as the inclusion of the faux circus tent structure. The Adventuredome, a 5-acre (2.0 ha) indoor amusement park located within a large pink glass dome connected to Circus Circus, offers rides such as the Canyon Blaster and El Loco roller coasters, along with midway and arcade games. Circus Circus added the amusement park in 1993 on property behind the resort, originally named Grand Slam Canyon until 1997. The resort features the Steak House, a popular restaurant that opened in 1982, replacing a spa area and winning several awards; during the 1990s, the two main restaurants were the Steak House and a buffet, which averaged about 13,000 diners per day, though readers of the Las Vegas Review-Journal voted it Las Vegas' worst for seven consecutive years starting in 2001; in 2021, part of the buffet was replaced with a food court including Dairy Queen, Einstein Bros. Bagels, Pick Up Stix, and Popeyes. Slots-A-Fun Casino, located in a separate building along the Las Vegas Strip directly south of the Circus Circus east entrance, opened in August 1971 by Jay Sarno, replacing a merry-go-round; management was assumed by Ross W. Miller in 1974, a former Circus Circus executive and father of future Nevada governor Bob Miller, who was reported to be leasing the premises from the Teamsters Union, which had provided some financing for Circus Circus. In 1975, Carl Thomas bought into the casino as an equal partner with Miller, who died that year; in 1979, Thomas was exposed for involvement in casino skimming on behalf of the Kansas City mob, with claims that the mob had a secret interest through Allen Dorfman, though the claim was never substantiated; Thomas's gaming licenses were revoked, and he was forced to sell his interests. Miller's estate and Thomas sold Slots-A-Fun to Circus Circus Hotels, Inc., owned by Bill Bennett and Bill Pennington, who operated the Circus Circus casino; their company later became Circus Circus Enterprises and then Mandalay Resort Group. MGM Mirage (later MGM Resorts International) acquired Mandalay Resort Group in 2005 and thus acquired Slots-A-Fun; as of 2014, it was one of the last casinos to offer coin-operated slot machines. Phil Ruffin purchased Circus Circus and Slots-A-Fun in 2019; the casino is known for its low-priced drinks and table games. In 1969, Circus Circus hosted an episode of The Ed Sullivan Show and appears in the 1970 film The Grasshopper. In the 1971 novel Fear and Loathing in Las Vegas, Hunter S. Thompson described Circus Circus as "the sixth Reich," noting its circus tent-like structure and carnival atmosphere; when adapted into a film in 1998, the fictional "Bazooko Circus" was used as a stand-in for Circus Circus, which had refused filming permission. Circus Circus is featured in the 1971 James Bond film Diamonds Are Forever, which includes key scenes in the casino and midway; Sarno has a cameo, and Tanya the elephant performs a slot machine trick. A year later, it appeared in an episode of Banacek titled "A Million the Hard Way," and made other film appearances in the 1970s, including Las Vegas Lady, Damnation Alley, and Corvette Summer. The 1999 film Baby Geniuses was partially shot at the Adventuredome, which stood in as the fictional Joyworld theme park. Circus Circus also appears in a 1998 King of the Hill episode, "Next of Shin," where Hank, Dale, and Bill search for Hank's father Cotton in Las Vegas. In the 2004 video game Grand Theft Auto: San Andreas, Circus Circus is known as Clown's Pocket; a recreation called the Ringmaster appears in the 2014 racing game The Crew near the northern end of the Las Vegas Strip. In 1993, a robbery occurred at Circus Circus when Heather Tallchief, a driver for an armored truck, stole $3 million intended for ATM distribution with the help of murderer Roberto Solis; they disappeared but Tallchief surrendered 12 years later. The robbery is detailed in a 2021 Netflix docuseries, Heist.
